sections.skill: Judge usefulness and correctness separately; expect variation

questions.prompt: A draft outline saves you an hour but has one wrong date. How would you describe it?

choices.text: Useful, but not fully correct until fixed
Useless, since it has an error
Correct and useful, so no edits needed

questions.correct_answer: Useful, but not fully correct until fixed
questions.intro: USEFUL and CORRECT are different questions. A draft can be useful (it saves time, gives you a structure or ideas) even if some facts in it are wrong, as long as you fix them. An answer can also be correct but not useful (accurate but off-topic, too technical, or missing what you needed). Judge both separately. Also expect that results may not REPEAT exactly: the same request can give different wording or even different facts on another day, after a product update, or with a different setting. If you need to rely on a result later, save the version you checked.

sections.skill: Compare a rough map sketch with a perfect map in another language

questions.prompt: The napkin sketch is...
questions.correct_answer: Useful but not fully correct
questions.intro: A friend sketches a ROUGH MAP on a napkin. It is not to scale and one street name is wrong, but it gets you to the party: USEFUL, though not fully correct. Another friend gives you a PERFECT MAP, but it is printed in a language you cannot read: CORRECT, but not useful to you. And if you ask the napkin friend to draw it again tomorrow, the sketch will look a little different. That is why you judge usefulness and correctness separately, and keep the version you checked.

questions.prompt: A tool worked well once for sorting invoices. Should you assume it will always work?

choices.text: No; test it on several examples over time
No; it will never work again

questions.correct_answer: No; test it on several examples over time
questions.intro: Because results can change, a one-time success is weak evidence that a tool will work for you every time. If you use a tool repeatedly for the same kind of task, keep a few test examples with known good answers and rerun them now and then. Record what you asked, what you got and what you checked. This makes your work reproducible: someone else, or you next month, can see how a result was produced and judge it, instead of trusting "the AI said so."
